slides: Welcome back. Now let's look at similarity in regular shapes.

slides.say: Remember, in a regular shape all the sides are equal, and all the angles are equal. A square and an equilateral triangle are regular shapes.

slides: Regular shapes of the same kind are always similar. Let's see why, and how it helps us.

slides.say: Why are they always similar? Think of a circle. Every circle in the world looks exactly the same. Only the size changes.

slides: It's the same with squares, with equilateral triangles and with regular hexagons. Each kind has only one shape.

slides.say: But the number of sides must be the same. A regular pentagon and a regular hexagon aren't similar. They're different shapes.
at: the number of sides must be the same

slides.say: Careful, other shapes are not always similar. Here are two rectangles. One is long and thin, and the other is almost a square.
And here are two right triangles. Their sharp angles are different, so they don't have the same shape.

slides: For shapes like these, we have to check. We'll learn how in the next lesson.

slides.say: First example, the equilateral triangle. Every equilateral triangle has three angles of sixty degrees. So all equilateral triangles are similar.

slides: Here the small triangle has side a, and the big one has side three a. The big one is an enlarged picture of the small one.

slides.say: How many small triangles fit inside the big one? Let's count. One, two, three, and so on, up to nine.
That's exactly what we learned in the last lesson. The linear ratio is one to three. So the area ratio is one squared to three squared, one to nine.
at: The linear ratio is one to three

slides.say: And the perimeters? A perimeter is a line, so it keeps the linear ratio. The perimeters are one to three too.
at: The perimeters are one to three

slides.say: Squares are similar too. Here the sides are four and seven.
at: Here the sides are four and seven

slides.say: Cutting the big square into small ones would be hard here. So we don't. We just use the rule. The area ratio is the linear ratio, squared.
Four squared is sixteen, and seven squared is forty-nine. So the areas are sixteen to forty-nine.
What does that mean? If the small square is sixteen square centimeters, the big one is forty-nine.
If the small square is thirty-two, that's double sixteen. So the big one is double forty-nine, ninety-eight.
So we think of it as sixteen ratio units against forty-nine ratio units. One unit can be any number, but it's the same number in both squares.
Let's use it. Say the small square is forty-eight. Then sixteen units are forty-eight.
So one unit is forty-eight divided by sixteen. That's three, because sixteen times three is forty-eight.
at: So one unit is forty-eight divided by

slides.say: The big square is forty-nine units. Forty times three is a hundred twenty, and nine times three is twenty-seven. So it's a hundred forty-seven.
at: The big square is forty-nine units

slides.say: A regular hexagon is a regular shape too. So all regular hexagons are similar.
Here's a small hexagon and a big hexagon. Their sides are five and six.

slides: What's the area ratio? Try to think about it before I say it.

slides.say: Twenty-five to thirty-six. Five squared is twenty-five, and six squared is thirty-six.

slides: We don't need to cut each hexagon into six equilateral triangles. The similarity already did the work.

slides.say: Now circles. Here the radii are two and five. So the linear ratio is two to five.
at: Here the radii are two and five

slides.say: The area ratio is two squared to five squared, four to twenty-five.
at: The area ratio is two squared

slides.say: Now careful. Say they tell us the small circumference is eight. What's the big circumference?

slides: A circumference is a line. So we stay with the linear ratio, and we don't square it.

slides.say: Five divided by two is two and a half. So the big circle is two and a half times the small one.
Eight times two is sixteen, and half of eight is four. Sixteen plus four is twenty. So the big circumference is twenty.
So we treat the circumference as a line, because that's what it is. Only areas get squared.
Regular shapes of the same kind are always similar, if they have the same number of sides.
at: Regular shapes of the same kind

slides.say: Lines, like sides, perimeters and circumferences, keep the linear ratio.
Areas get the linear ratio squared. And with ratio units, we turn the ratio into real numbers.
at: Areas get the linear ratio squared
